passages.title: The Night of Decree: revelation, angels, peace
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah al-Qadr is a short surah about one night — the night on which Allah sent down the Qur'an, a night whose worship Allah declares better than a thousand months, on which His angels come down to the earth, and which is peace until the break of dawn. The five ayat move as one arc: **revelation** (ayah 1), **magnification** (ayah 2), **worth** (ayah 3), **descent** (ayah 4), and **peace** (ayah 5). What holds them together is that every one of them is about the same night, and each adds a further reason why it is called *the Night of Qadr*.

## Why the surah was revealed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports an occasion of revelation that opens the surah beautifully. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid — as a *mursal* hadith, meaning a report whose chain is incomplete, not naming the Companion who heard it from the Prophet ﷺ — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was told about a warrior in the cause of religion from among the Children of Israel who carried his weapons of war on his shoulders for a thousand months and never once laid down his arms. The Companions were amazed when they heard this. On that occasion this surah was revealed, describing that worship in the Night of Qadr, granted to this Ummah, exceeds by more than a thousand months of the jihad that warrior persistently fought. A second narration of Mujahid, cited in Ibn Jarir, describes a worshipper from the Children of Israel who worshipped Allah the whole night, and as soon as dawn broke would arm himself and fight the whole day — and this continued consecutively for a thousand months.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (quoting Mazhari) draws the point out: this shows the superiority of the Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ, and that the Night of Qadr is a special characteristic of this ummah.

## Ayah 1: "Indeed, We sent it down"

Allah begins by attributing the revelation to Himself — *We sent it down*. Ibn Kathir connects this with two other ayat: *We sent it down on a blessed night* (44:3), and *The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an* (2:185). Put together, the blessed night of Sūrah ad-Dukhān is the Night of Qadr, and it occurs during the month of Ramadan.

**How was the Qur'an "sent down" on one night?** Ibn 'Abbas and others said: Allah sent the Qur'an down all at one time from the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfūz*) to the House of Might (*Bayt al-ʿIzzah*), which is in the heaven of this world; then it came down in parts to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ based upon the incidents that occurred over a period of twenty-three years. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this as the first of two possible meanings — with Jibrā'īl (peace be upon him) bringing it down piecemeal as circumstances required — and offers a second: that the *first* revelation, the opening ayat of Sūrah 96, took place in Ramadan on the Night of Qadr while the Prophet ﷺ was at his devotion in the cave of Hirā', with the rest of the Qur'an revealed little by little according to the need of different occasions.

## Ayah 2: the question that magnifies

*And what will make you realize what the Night of Glory is?* Ibn Kathir explains that with these words Allah magnified the status of the Night of Al-Qadr — the night He chose for the revelation of the Mighty Qur'an. He reads this ayah together with the one after it, so the answer to the question is given in the ayah that follows: this night is better than a thousand months.

## What "Qadr" means

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two senses of the word, and both are true of the night.

**Qadr as greatness, honour and dignity.** Zuhri and other scholars assigned this meaning to it: the night is called the Night of Qadr because it is a night of greatness, honour, majesty and dignity. Abu Bakr Warrāq added a moving second layer — the night is so called because a person *becomes* a man of honour and dignity on account of repentance, seeking pardon and righteous acts during this night, whereas before it he might have lacked honour and dignity on account of the unrighteous life he had led.

**Qadr as predestination.** On this reading, the destiny of individuals and nations that was decided in pre-eternity is assigned on this night to the relevant angels appointed for cosmic planning: every person's age, death, sustenance, rain and other things, measured out to be implemented for a complete year from one Ramadan to the next. If someone is destined to perform Hajj in the coming year, it is prescribed. According to Ibn 'Abbas, there are four angels in charge of this: Isrāfīl, Mīkā'īl, ʿIzrā'īl and Jibrā'īl. This is the sense of Allah's words *In that night, every wise thing is decided* (44:4).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a difference here worth naming honestly. According to the overwhelming body of Qur'an scholars, the "blessed night" of 44:3 refers to the Night of Qadr. Some scholars, however, hold that it refers to the fifteenth night of Shaʿbān, *Laylat al-Barā'ah*, the Night of Immunity. The two may be reconciled by holding that the initial divine decrees are decided on the Night of Immunity, and the details are recorded and handed over to the relevant angels on the Night of Qadr — supported by a narration of Ibn 'Abbas that Baghawi recorded on the authority of Abū ad-Duhā.

## Ayah 3: better than a thousand months

Ibn Kathir cites what Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah, that when Ramadan would come the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would say: *"Verily, the month of Ramadan has come to you all. It is a blessed month, which Allah has obligated you all to fast. During it the gates of Paradise are opened, the gates of Hell are closed and the devils are shackled. In it there is a night that is better than one thousand months. Whoever is deprived of its good, then he has truly been deprived."* An-Nasā'ī recorded this same hadith.

A thousand months amounts to eighty-three years and four months. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes an important point about the figure: here and elsewhere in the Qur'an it does not signify a precise number, but simply denotes a very large or high number — Allah alone knows how much more or better it truly is.

## Ayah 4: the angels and the Rūh come down

*Therein descend the angels and the Rūh by their Lord's permission with every matter.* Ibn Kathir explains that the angels descend **in abundance** on this night due to its abundant blessings — they descend with the descending of blessings and mercy, just as they descend when the Qur'an is recited, surround the circles of *dhikr* (remembrance of Allah), and lower their wings with true respect for the student of knowledge.

**Who is "ar-Rūh"?** Ibn Kathir says that in reference to ar-Rūh, it is said that here it means the angel Jibrīl; the wording of the ayah is therefore a method of naming the distinct individual — Jibrīl — separately from the general group, the angels. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise says the Spirit here refers to Jibrā'īl (peace be upon him).

Two narrations are cited on this descent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays from Mazhari that Anas narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that when the Night of Qadr occurs, Jibrā'īl descends to the earth with a huge throng of angels, and all of them pray for every servant of Allah, man or woman, busy in salah or dhikr, to be blessed by Allah. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that all the angels resident at the Lote Tree of the Uttermost Boundary descend under the leadership of Jibrā'īl and greet every believer, man or woman, except one who takes wine or eats pork. Ibn Kathir separately cites what Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah, that the angels who are on the earth during that night are more numerous than the number of pebbles; Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad was alone in recording this hadith and that there is nothing wrong with its chain of narration.

**"With every matter."** The Arabic *min kulli amr* is read in two ways. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the preposition *min* is used here in the sense of "with" — so the ayah means the angels bring down, during the Night of Qadr, the decree for everything destined to occur in the coming year. This matches what Ibn Kathir reports from Qatadah and others: "The matters are determined during it, and the times of death and provisions are measured out during it." The second reading — from Mujahid and others — treats *min kulli amr* as syntactically related to the word *salām* in ayah 5, so the meaning becomes: the night is a security from every evil, harm and calamity.

**"By their Lord's permission."** The ayah itself frames the descent this way: the angels come down by the permission of their Lord, carrying what He has decreed.

## Ayah 5: "It is all peace, until the break of dawn"

The Arabic *salāmun hiya* is compact and total. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from Qurtubi) says the word *salām* here stands for a complete sentence: it is all peace, equanimity and complete goodness, having no evil in it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds (from Mazhari) that some scholars treat *salāmun* as a sentence qualifying *min kulli amr*, meaning that the angels come with every such matter which is good and peace.

Ibn Kathir gathers the early explanations:

- **Mujahid**: "It is security in which Shaytan cannot do any evil or any harm."
- **Ash-Shaʿbī** (reported by Saʿīd bin Mansūr): the angels give the greetings of peace during the Night of Al-Qadr to the people in the masjids until the coming of Fajr.
- **Qatadah and Ibn Zayd**: "This means all of it is good and there is no evil in it until the coming of Fajr."

The closing words *until the break of dawn* matter practically. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the blessings of this night are not restricted to any particular part of it: they start descending at the fall of night and continue till the break of dawn. It also observes that on account of geographical positions the time varies from place to place, so the Night of Qadr does not occur in all regions of the world simultaneously — people of each location should calculate and consecrate the night and receive its blessings according to their own position. And Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.

## Which night is it?

Both commentaries treat this at length, because the Prophet ﷺ was caused to forget the exact night.

It has been reported that Abu Saʿīd al-Khudrī described how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed *i'tikāf* (secluded worship in the masjid) during the first ten nights of Ramadan, and the Companions with him; then Jibrīl came and said, "That which you are seeking is in front of you." So he performed i'tikāf during the middle ten days; Jibrīl came again: "That which you are seeking is ahead of you." So on the morning of the twentieth of Ramadan he ﷺ stood and gave a sermon: *"Whoever performed i'tikāf with me, let him come back, for verily I saw the Night of Al-Qadr, and I was caused to forget it, and indeed it is during the last ten nights. It is during an odd night and I saw myself as if I were prostrating in mud and water."* The roof of the masjid was made of dried palm-tree leaves and they saw nothing in the sky — then a patch of wind-driven clouds came and it rained, and he ﷺ led them in prayer until they saw the traces of mud and water on his blessed forehead, which confirmed his dream. Al-Bukhari and Muslim both recorded it in the Two Sahihs. Ash-Shāfiʿī said, "This hadith is the most authentic of what has been reported."

Beyond that, the reports point to different odd nights, and Ibn Kathir lays them out with attribution rather than forcing one answer:

- **The last ten, odd nights generally**: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites 'A'ishah's narration recorded in the Sahih of Bukhari — *"Look for the Night of Qadr in the last ten nights of Ramadan"* — and Ibn 'Umar's, recorded in Sahih Muslim — *"Search for it in the last ten odd nights of Ramadan."*
- **The 23rd**: due to a hadith narrated from 'Abdullah bin Unays in Sahih Muslim.
- **The 25th**: Al-Bukhari recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, *"Seek it in the last ten nights of Ramadan. In the ninth it still remains, in the seventh it still remains, in the fifth it still remains"* — many have explained this to refer to the odd nights, which Ibn Kathir calls the most apparent and most popular explanation.
- **The 27th**: Muslim recorded in his Sahih from Ubay bin Kaʿb that the Prophet ﷺ mentioned that it was on the twenty-seventh night. Imam Ahmad recorded that Zirr asked Ubayy how he knew; Ubayy replied that it was by a sign the Prophet ﷺ informed them of — that the sun rises the next day having no rays on it. Muslim has also recorded this.
- **The 29th, or any odd night**: Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal recorded from 'Ubādah bin as-Sāmit that he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the Night of Decree, and he replied, *"Seek it in Ramadan in the last ten nights. For verily, it is during the odd nights, the twenty-first, or the twenty-third, or the twenty-fifth, or the twenty-seventh, or the twenty-ninth, or during the last night."*

Ibn Kathir also cites a report describing the night's signs — that it is pure and glowing as if there were a bright, tranquil, calm moon during it, neither cold nor hot, and that the sun appears the next morning smooth, having no rays on it, just like the moon on a full-moon night — but he adds, with a muhaddith's honesty, that although the chain of narration is good, in its text there are some oddities and in some of its wordings there are things that are objectionable. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a caution of its own: on this night some people experience and witness special lights, but this is not experienced by all and sundry, nor is it part of the blessings and reward of the night, so people should not concern themselves about it.

**The conclusion the scholars reached.** At-Tirmidhi recorded from Abu Qilābah that the Night of Al-Qadr *moves around* from year to year throughout the last ten nights. Ibn Kathir notes that this view has also been recorded by Malik, ath-Thawrī, Ahmad bin Hanbal, Ishaq bin Rāhūyah, Abu Thawr, al-Muzanī, Abu Bakr bin Khuzaymah and others, and has also been related from ash-Shāfiʿī — and Ibn Kathir says "this is most likely. And Allah knows best." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that about forty opinions are recorded, and that Mazhari holds the most authentic to be exactly this: the last ten nights of Ramadan with no fixed date, any of the last ten odd nights, alternating from year to year — the 21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th and 29th — so that all the apparently conflicting authentic narrations are reconciled without any convoluted interpretation. (Imam Shāfiʿī is reported with two opinions: in one he sides with the majority, in the other he holds that the night is fixed and does not alternate.) Ibn Kathir also records that Abu Dawud titled a chapter in his Sunan "Clarification that the Night of Al-Qadr occurs during every Ramadan" and reported from 'Abdullah bin 'Umar that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about it and said, *"It occurs during every Ramadan"* — the men of the chain are all reliable, though Abu Dawud said that Shuʿbah and Sufyān both considered it a statement of the Companion rather than of the Prophet ﷺ.

## Living these ayat

The uncertainty is the instruction. Since the night could be any of the last ten odd nights, the way to be sure of catching it is to seek it across all of them, as the narrations command.

**Stand in prayer.** It is confirmed in the Two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Whoever stands in prayer during the Night of Al-Qadr with faith and expecting reward from Allah, he will be forgiven for his previous sins."* Two conditions are attached in the wording itself: faith, and expecting the reward from Allah.

**If you cannot stand all night, do not stay away.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records as a ruling that whoever performs the ʿIshā' and Fajr prayers in congregation will receive the blessings and reward of the Night of Qadr, citing what is recorded in the Sahih of Muslim from 'Uthman, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If a person performs his ʿIshā' salah in congregation, he will attain the blessings of spending half the night in devotion; and if he performs Fajr salah in congregation, he will attain the blessings of spending the entire night in devotion." And the more one performs acts of worship in this night, the more of its blessings one receives.

**Ask to be pardoned.** Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad narrated from 'A'ishah that she said, "O Messenger of Allah! If I find the Night of Al-Qadr, what should I say?" He ﷺ replied: *"Say: Allāhumma innaka ʿafuwwun tuhibbu al-ʿafwa faʿfu ʿannī* — O Allah! Verily, You are the Oft-Pardoning, You love to pardon, so pardon me." At-Tirmidhi, an-Nasā'ī and Ibn Majah have all recorded it; at-Tirmidhi said it is *hasan sahih* — his own grading term for a report he holds to be both sound and reliably transmitted — and al-Hakim recorded it in his *Mustadrak* with a different chain, saying it is authentic according to the criteria of al-Bukhari and Muslim. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same supplication from Qurtubi. Notice what she was taught to ask for: not wealth or ease, but *ʿafw*, Allah's pardon. And notice the reason given for asking it, in the words of the supplication itself: because He *loves* to pardon.

**Do not be among the deprived.** The warning in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah is stark: *"Whoever is deprived of its good, then he has truly been deprived."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports another narration to the same effect: whoever is deprived of the good of the Night of Qadr is in fact deprived of all good. Every Ramadan carries a night whose worship is better than a thousand months — eighty-three years and four months by the count, and a figure that stands for an immensity only Allah knows. Ayah 5 promises that it is peace, unbroken, until the break of dawn.
